Go and secure it as best you know how.”"}]},{"verse":66,"paragraph_start":false,"segments":[{"speaker":"narrator","text":"So they went and secured the tomb, sealing the stone and setting the guard."}]}],"notes":[{"verse":3,"phrase":"handed him over","lemma":"παραδίδωμι","kind":"departure","traditional":"betrayed him","note":"The Greek verb is the ordinary word for transferring someone into another’s custody, and Matthew uses the same verb for what Judas does, what the priests do to Jesus before Pilate (verse 2), and what Pilate does (verse 26). Most English versions say “betrayed” when Judas is the subject; that names the treachery the context supplies but hides the chain of handings-over. Standard lexicons give “hand over” as the basic sense, though some scholars defend “betray” as a legitimate contextual meaning."},{"verse":5,"phrase":"sanctuary","lemma":"ναός","kind":"departure","traditional":"temple","note":"Greek has two words that English Bibles usually both translate “temple”: one for the whole complex with its courts, and this one for the sanctuary building itself. It is rendered “sanctuary” here so that the charge in verse 40 and the curtain in verse 51 visibly use the same word. Most versions say “temple”, and this verse is often cited as a looser use of the word, since Judas could not have entered the inner building; he may have thrown the coins toward it or into its precincts."},{"verse":9,"phrase":"Jeremiah the prophet","lemma":"","kind":"background","traditional":"","note":"The wording is closest to Zechariah 11:12–13, where thirty pieces of silver are thrown to the potter in the house of the Lord. Matthew names Jeremiah, most likely because the quotation is blended with themes from that book: the potter, a burial ground linked with innocent blood, and the purchase of a field (Jeremiah 18–19 and 32). The precise explanation is debated."},{"verse":11,"phrase":"You say so","lemma":"","kind":"ambiguity","traditional":"","note":"The Greek is literally “You are saying it.” It can be heard as a plain yes or as a guarded reply (“the words are yours”); it is not a denial. Most interpreters take it as a qualified assent that leaves the meaning of “king” with the questioner."},{"verse":16,"phrase":"Jesus Barabbas","lemma":"","kind":"textual","traditional":"Barabbas","note":"Most manuscripts read simply “Barabbas” here and in verse 17, and most English versions have traditionally followed them. A smaller group of witnesses reads “Jesus Barabbas”, a reading already known to Origen in the third century, and many scholars think the name “Jesus” was original and was dropped by copyists out of reverence. The Greek edition translated here prints the longer reading, which makes Pilate’s question a choice between two men named Jesus."},{"verse":17,"phrase":"Messiah","lemma":"Χριστός","kind":"departure","traditional":"Christ","note":"The Greek word is a title for the anointed king Israel expected, and Pilate uses it here as a title, not as part of a name. “Messiah” conveys that to a modern reader, for whom “Christ” can sound like a surname. Several modern translations make the same choice in the Gospels."},{"verse":25,"phrase":"His blood be on us and on our children","lemma":"","kind":"background","traditional":"","note":"This is a biblical formula for accepting responsibility for a death (compare 2 Samuel 1:16 and Jeremiah 26:15). In the narrative it is spoken by the crowd gathered before Pilate, though Matthew’s word for “the people” is the one he generally uses for Israel as a nation. The verse has a long history of being misused to assign guilt to Jews of every generation, a reading that most interpreters today reject."},{"verse":38,"phrase":"bandits","lemma":"λῃστής","kind":"departure","traditional":"robbers (“thieves” in the King James Version)","note":"The Greek word denotes someone who robs with violence, such as a brigand or highwayman, and is distinct from the word for a thief who steals by stealth. It was also applied to insurgents, and some translations say “rebels” here; that reading is possible but not certain. Most modern versions use “robbers”."},{"verse":39,"phrase":"hurled insults at","lemma":"βλασφημέω","kind":"departure","traditional":"reviled (the Greek verb is the source of “blaspheme”)","note":"In the period this verb meant abusive speech against anyone, not only against God, whereas modern English “blaspheme” is limited to irreverence toward the divine. Here passers-by jeer at Jesus to his face, so “hurled insults at” gives the sense. English versions vary among “reviled”, “derided” and “hurled insults”."},{"verse":45,"phrase":"the sixth hour","lemma":"","kind":"background","traditional":"","note":"Hours were counted from sunrise, so the sixth hour is about noon and the ninth about three in the afternoon. The word translated “land” can also mean “earth”; whether Matthew means the region or the whole world is not certain."},{"verse":46,"phrase":"My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?","lemma":"","kind":"background","traditional":"","note":"These are the opening words of Psalm 22, which Matthew gives first in a Semitic form (largely Aramaic, with the Hebrew-sounding “Eli”) and then in Greek. The same psalm lies behind the divided clothing, the shaking heads and the taunt in verse 43. “Eli” (“my God”) sounds like a short form of Elijah’s name, which explains the bystanders’ reaction; Elijah was popularly expected to come to the help of the righteous in distress."},{"verse":52,"phrase":"holy ones","lemma":"ἅγιος","kind":"departure","traditional":"saints","note":"The traditional “saints” now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue. The Greek word means people set apart for God and echoes the Septuagint’s language for Israel; here it refers to the faithful dead. Many translations keep “saints”, and others use “holy people”."},{"verse":54,"phrase":"God’s Son","lemma":"","kind":"ambiguity","traditional":"the Son of God","note":"The Greek has no article and could be read as “a son of a god”, which is how a Roman soldier might naturally have meant it. Matthew’s readers, however, would hear the title used throughout the Gospel and thrown at Jesus in verses 40 and 43, and Greek grammar allows a definite sense without the article. “God’s Son” leaves the phrase about as open as the Greek does."},{"verse":62,"phrase":"the Preparation","lemma":"παρασκευή","kind":"background","traditional":"","note":"“Preparation” was the usual name for the day before the Sabbath, that is, Friday. The day after it is therefore the Sabbath, which Matthew does not name directly as the day the chief priests and Pharisees went to the governor."},{"verse":65,"phrase":"You have a guard","lemma":"ἔχω","kind":"ambiguity","traditional":"","note":"The Greek verb can be a statement (“You have a guard”) or a command (“Take a guard”). As a command, Pilate grants them Roman soldiers; as a statement, it may mean the same or may refer them to their own temple police. The word for “guard” is a Latin military term, and in 28:14 the guards are answerable to the governor, which favors Roman soldiers."}],"candidates":[{"lemma":"γραμματεύς","rendering":"scribes","verse":41,"reason":"Recurs throughout the Gospels and Acts, and versions divide between “scribes”, “teachers of the law” and “legal experts”, so readers would be confused by variation."},{"lemma":"διακονέω","rendering":"serving","verse":55,"reason":"Occurs across the Gospels, Acts and letters with renderings ranging from “serve” and “minister to” to “provide for” and “wait on”, and the choice affects how the women’s and others’ roles are understood."},{"lemma":"ἐγείρω","rendering":"be raised","verse":52,"reason":"The passive forms used of resurrection can be rendered “was raised” or “rose”, and the choice between them needs to be uniform across the Gospels, Acts and Paul."},{"lemma":"ἰδού","rendering":"look","verse":51,"reason":"Extremely frequent in narrative and speech, and translators vary among “behold”, “look”, “see”, “suddenly” or omission, so a single policy is needed."},{"lemma":"πραιτώριον","rendering":"headquarters","verse":27,"reason":"Appears in all the Passion narratives, Acts and Philippians, and is variously rendered “praetorium”, “governor’s headquarters”, “palace” and “imperial guard”, so parallel passages need to match."}]}

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When morning came, all the chief priests and the elders of the people conferred together against Jesus, to put him to death.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They bound him, led him away, and handed him over to Pilate the governor.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Judas, who had handed him over, saw that Jesus had been condemned. Filled with remorse, he returned the thirty silver coins to the chief priests and elders,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I have sinned by handing over innocent blood.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But they said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “What is that to us? See to it yourself.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Throwing the silver coins into the sanctuary, he left; then he went away and hanged himself.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The chief priests took the silver coins and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “It is not permitted to put these into the temple treasury, since they are the price of blood.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After conferring together, they used the money to buy the Potter’s Field as a burial place for foreigners.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: That is why that field has been called the Field of Blood to this day.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then what was spoken through Jeremiah the prophet was fulfilled:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “And they took the thirty silver coins, the price of the one on whom a price had been set, on whom some of the sons of Israel had set a price,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: and they gave them for the potter’s field, as the Lord directed me.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now Jesus stood before the governor, and the governor questioned him, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Are you the king of the Jews?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “You say so.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And when he was accused by the chief priests and elders, he answered nothing.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Pilate said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Do you not hear how many things they are testifying against you?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he gave him no answer, not even to a single charge, so that the governor was greatly amazed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now at each festival the governor was in the habit of releasing to the crowd one prisoner, whichever one they wanted.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: At that time they were holding a notorious prisoner called Jesus Barabbas.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So when they had gathered, Pilate said to them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Which one do you want me to release to you: Jesus Barabbas, or Jesus who is called Messiah?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For he knew that it was out of envy that they had handed him over.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: While he was sitting on the judgment seat, his wife sent word to him:

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Have nothing to do with that righteous man, for today I have suffered a great deal in a dream because of him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the chief priests and the elders persuaded the crowds to ask for Barabbas and to have Jesus destroyed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The governor spoke up and said to them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Which of the two do you want me to release to you?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Barabbas.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Pilate said to them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Then what am I to do with Jesus who is called Messiah?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They all said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Let him be crucified!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Why? What evil has he done?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But they shouted all the louder,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Let him be crucified!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Pilate saw that he was getting nowhere, and that a riot was starting instead, he took water and washed his hands in front of the crowd, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I am innocent of this man’s blood. See to it yourselves.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And all the people answered,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “His blood be on us and on our children!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he released Barabbas to them; but Jesus he had flogged, and handed him over to be crucified.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then the governor’s soldiers took Jesus into the headquarters and gathered the whole cohort around him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They stripped him and put a scarlet cloak on him,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and they wove a crown out of thorns and put it on his head, and a reed in his right hand. Kneeling before him, they mocked him, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Hail, king of the Jews!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They spat on him, took the reed, and kept striking him on the head.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they had finished mocking him, they stripped him of the cloak, put his own clothes on him, and led him away to crucify him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As they were going out, they came upon a man from Cyrene named Simon, and they pressed him into service to carry his cross.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they came to a place called Golgotha, which means Place of a Skull,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: they gave him wine mixed with gall to drink; but after tasting it, he refused to drink.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they had crucified him, they divided his clothes among themselves by casting lots,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and sitting down, they kept watch over him there.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Above his head they put the charge against him in writing: “This is Jesus, the king of the Jews.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then two bandits were crucified with him, one on his right and one on his left.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Those passing by hurled insults at him, shaking their heads

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “You who would destroy the sanctuary and build it in three days, save yourself! If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In the same way the chief priests also, together with the scribes and elders, were mocking him and saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “He saved others; himself he cannot save. He is the king of Israel! Let him come down now from the cross, and we will believe in him.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: He has put his trust in God; let God rescue him now, if he wants him. For he said, ‘I am God’s Son.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And in the same way the bandits who were crucified with him also taunted him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: From the sixth hour, darkness came over the whole land until the ninth hour.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: About the ninth hour Jesus cried out with a loud voice,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: that is,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Some of those standing there heard it and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “This man is calling Elijah.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: At once one of them ran and got a sponge, filled it with sour wine, put it on a reed, and offered it to him to drink.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the rest said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Wait! Let us see whether Elijah comes to save him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Jesus cried out again with a loud voice and gave up his spirit.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And look, the curtain of the sanctuary was split in two from top to bottom. The earth shook, the rocks were split,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: the tombs were opened, and many bodies of the holy ones who had fallen asleep were raised;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and coming out of the tombs after his resurrection, they entered the holy city and appeared to many.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the centurion and those with him who were keeping watch over Jesus saw the earthquake and what was taking place, they were terrified and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Truly this man was God’s Son!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Many women were there, watching from a distance; they had followed Jesus from Galilee, serving him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Among them were Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joseph, and the mother of the sons of Zebedee.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When evening came, a rich man from Arimathea arrived, named Joseph, who had himself become a disciple of Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus. Then Pilate ordered it to be given to him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Joseph took the body, wrapped it in a clean linen cloth,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and laid it in his own new tomb, which he had cut in the rock. Then he rolled a large stone against the entrance of the tomb and went away.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Mary Magdalene and the other Mary were there, sitting opposite the tomb.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The next day, the one after the Preparation, the chief priests and the Pharisees gathered before Pilate

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Sir, we remember that while he was still alive that deceiver said, ‘After three days I will be raised.’

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: So give orders for the tomb to be secured until the third day; otherwise his disciples may come and steal him and tell the people, ‘He has been raised from the dead,’ and the last deception will be worse than the first.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Pilate said to them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “You have a guard. Go and secure it as best you know how.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So they went and secured the tomb, sealing the stone and setting the guard.

notes.note: The Greek verb is the ordinary word for transferring someone into another’s custody, and Matthew uses the same verb for what Judas does, what the priests do to Jesus before Pilate (verse 2), and what Pilate does (verse 26). Most English versions say “betrayed” when Judas is the subject; that names the treachery the context supplies but hides the chain of handings-over. Standard lexicons give “hand over” as the basic sense, though some scholars defend “betray” as a legitimate contextual meaning.

Greek has two words that English Bibles usually both translate “temple”: one for the whole complex with its courts, and this one for the sanctuary building itself. It is rendered “sanctuary” here so that the charge in verse 40 and the curtain in verse 51 visibly use the same word. Most versions say “temple”, and this verse is often cited as a looser use of the word, since Judas could not have entered the inner building; he may have thrown the coins toward it or into its precincts.

The wording is closest to Zechariah 11:12–13, where thirty pieces of silver are thrown to the potter in the house of the Lord. Matthew names Jeremiah, most likely because the quotation is blended with themes from that book: the potter, a burial ground linked with innocent blood, and the purchase of a field (Jeremiah 18–19 and 32). The precise explanation is debated.

The Greek is literally “You are saying it.” It can be heard as a plain yes or as a guarded reply (“the words are yours”); it is not a denial. Most interpreters take it as a qualified assent that leaves the meaning of “king” with the questioner.

Most manuscripts read simply “Barabbas” here and in verse 17, and most English versions have traditionally followed them. A smaller group of witnesses reads “Jesus Barabbas”, a reading already known to Origen in the third century, and many scholars think the name “Jesus” was original and was dropped by copyists out of reverence. The Greek edition translated here prints the longer reading, which makes Pilate’s question a choice between two men named Jesus.

The Greek word is a title for the anointed king Israel expected, and Pilate uses it here as a title, not as part of a name. “Messiah” conveys that to a modern reader, for whom “Christ” can sound like a surname. Several modern translations make the same choice in the Gospels.

notes.phrase: His blood be on us and on our children
notes.note: This is a biblical formula for accepting responsibility for a death (compare 2 Samuel 1:16 and Jeremiah 26:15). In the narrative it is spoken by the crowd gathered before Pilate, though Matthew’s word for “the people” is the one he generally uses for Israel as a nation. The verse has a long history of being misused to assign guilt to Jews of every generation, a reading that most interpreters today reject.

notes.traditional: robbers (“thieves” in the King James Version)
notes.note: The Greek word denotes someone who robs with violence, such as a brigand or highwayman, and is distinct from the word for a thief who steals by stealth. It was also applied to insurgents, and some translations say “rebels” here; that reading is possible but not certain. Most modern versions use “robbers”.

notes.traditional: reviled (the Greek verb is the source of “blaspheme”)
notes.note: In the period this verb meant abusive speech against anyone, not only against God, whereas modern English “blaspheme” is limited to irreverence toward the divine. Here passers-by jeer at Jesus to his face, so “hurled insults at” gives the sense. English versions vary among “reviled”, “derided” and “hurled insults”.

Hours were counted from sunrise, so the sixth hour is about noon and the ninth about three in the afternoon. The word translated “land” can also mean “earth”; whether Matthew means the region or the whole world is not certain.

notes.phrase: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?
notes.note: These are the opening words of Psalm 22, which Matthew gives first in a Semitic form (largely Aramaic, with the Hebrew-sounding “Eli”) and then in Greek. The same psalm lies behind the divided clothing, the shaking heads and the taunt in verse 43. “Eli” (“my God”) sounds like a short form of Elijah’s name, which explains the bystanders’ reaction; Elijah was popularly expected to come to the help of the righteous in distress.

The traditional “saints” now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue. The Greek word means people set apart for God and echoes the Septuagint’s language for Israel; here it refers to the faithful dead. Many translations keep “saints”, and others use “holy people”.

The Greek has no article and could be read as “a son of a god”, which is how a Roman soldier might naturally have meant it. Matthew’s readers, however, would hear the title used throughout the Gospel and thrown at Jesus in verses 40 and 43, and Greek grammar allows a definite sense without the article. “God’s Son” leaves the phrase about as open as the Greek does.

“Preparation” was the usual name for the day before the Sabbath, that is, Friday. The day after it is therefore the Sabbath, which Matthew does not name directly as the day the chief priests and Pharisees went to the governor.

The Greek verb can be a statement (“You have a guard”) or a command (“Take a guard”). As a command, Pilate grants them Roman soldiers; as a statement, it may mean the same or may refer them to their own temple police. The word for “guard” is a Latin military term, and in 28:14 the guards are answerable to the governor, which favors Roman soldiers.

candidates.reason: Recurs throughout the Gospels and Acts, and versions divide between “scribes”, “teachers of the law” and “legal experts”, so readers would be confused by variation.

Occurs across the Gospels, Acts and letters with renderings ranging from “serve” and “minister to” to “provide for” and “wait on”, and the choice affects how the women’s and others’ roles are understood.
The passive forms used of resurrection can be rendered “was raised” or “rose”, and the choice between them needs to be uniform across the Gospels, Acts and Paul.
Extremely frequent in narrative and speech, and translators vary among “behold”, “look”, “see”, “suddenly” or omission, so a single policy is needed.
Appears in all the Passion narratives, Acts and Philippians, and is variously rendered “praetorium”, “governor’s headquarters”, “palace” and “imperial guard”, so parallel passages need to match.
